source.title: LUCID-SAE: Learning Unified Vision-Language Sparse Codes for Interpretable Concept Discovery
source.authors: Di-Fei Gu; Yun-He Gao; Gerasimos Chatzoudis; Zi-Han Dong; Guo-Ning Zhang; Bang-Wei Guo; Yang Zhou; Mu Zhou; Dimitris N. Metaxas

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses neuron interpretability and reports interpretations of learned SAE features, but it does not test the claim versions about native neuron poles, their prevalence, or explanation validation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports qualitative semantic clusters for 12 randomly selected shared LUCID-SAE features (Table 5). These are learned SAE features, not an audit of the backbone model's own neuron poles, and the paper does not estimate the share with one or multiple jobs. Its reconstruction and grounding comparisons do not test the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper trains a unified vision-language SAE on SigLIP ViT-B/16 and interprets its learned SAE dictionary units (called 'neurons'). It never audits the backbone's native neurons, measures shares of one-job neurons, builds neuron-based attribution graphs, or scores explanations by held-out activation prediction. It mentions neuron polysemanticity only in related work, citing superposition literature. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that LUCID's unified shared/private SAE improves reconstruction and cross-modal predictability, that OT/GCMT improves patch-level grounding, and that structured shared codes reduce clustering degeneracy. They also conclude that the automated pipeline finds coherent semantic clusters spanning objects, scenes, actions, attributes and spatial relations. They draw no conclusion about native neuron interpretability shares.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains a unified Top-k sparse autoencoder with shared and private codes plus cross-modal transport alignment, then clusters text concepts associated with learned features. It does not perform the Qwen3 neuron-pole audit or test explanations on held-out activations.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that shared/private capacity, Top-k sparsity, Global Semantic Lock, and GCMT change reconstruction, clustering-degeneracy, and grounding metrics; it does not show these settings changing a claim-version outcome.

fits_no_version.finding: In 12 randomly selected shared LUCID-SAE units on SigLIP ViT-B/16, each is reported to have a dominant semantic cluster of text concepts. Selection used a minimum concept-hit count and a cluster purity ≥0.55 filter. The dominant clusters often include off-theme terms.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learned shared SAE features in a vision-language model can be assigned coherent semantic themes by automated clustering of associated text concepts.

record.problems: The interpretation examples are qualitative and limited to 12 randomly selected features; the paper filters for minimum concept hits and dominant-cluster purity of at least 0.55. It does not report an independent held-out test of whether the interpretations predict activations.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B or other native neuron-pole audit; no shares reported.
No language models or scale comparison; no native-neuron shares.
No InceptionV1 or canonical polysemantic neuron reanalysis.
No comparison of architecture, regularization or tools against native-neuron interpretability share.
No attribution graphs from native neurons; no replacement-model comparison.
No held-out prediction test of activating-example explanations.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only': the paper only restates the standard superposition/polysemanticity view in related work and does not argue about the claim. 'Neuron' in this paper refers to SAE dictionary units. The purity ≥0.55 filter means the 12 examples are not an unbiased audit even of SAE features.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit Qwen3-32B native neuron poles or report proportions with one job, two related jobs, or unexplained poles.
Does not measure neuron-job shares across language models, dense or mixture-of-experts models, or model scales.
Does not study InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose, or recursive generalization.
Does not compare architecture, regularization, or tools as causes of native-neuron interpretability shares, and does not estimate shares for InceptionV1-sized vision models.
Does not evaluate attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons or compare them with a trained replacement model.
Does not test whether explanations derived from activating examples predict held-out activations.
Does not score explanations by simulating neuron activations on new text.
